notes.definition: Reaction time is the time between a person detecting a stimulus (such as a hazard on the road) and responding to it. Typical human reaction times range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
explanation: Reaction times vary from person to person, and the same person's reaction time can vary from moment to moment. Typical values range from about 0.2 s to 0.9 s. For a driver, reaction time is the time between seeing a hazard and starting to press the brake pedal. During this time the car continues at a constant speed, so a longer reaction time means a longer thinking distance, since thinking distance = speed × reaction time.

A driver's reaction time is increased by tiredness, alcohol and drugs (including some prescription medicines). Distractions such as using a mobile phone, adjusting a sat nav, eating or talking to passengers also affect a driver's ability to react, because the driver may take longer to notice the hazard. Age and experience can also make a difference. All of these factors increase the thinking distance, and so the stopping distance, but they do not change the braking distance.

A simple way to measure reaction time is the ruler drop test. A partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark level with the gap between the catcher's thumb and first finger. Without warning, the partner lets go and the catcher closes their fingers to catch the ruler as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls before it is caught is read from the scale. The further the ruler falls, the longer the reaction time. The distance can be converted to a time using a conversion table or graph, because the ruler accelerates at a known rate (9.8 m/s²) as it falls.

To get valid results, repeat the test several times, ignore any anomalous results and calculate a mean. Control variables such as which hand is used, the starting position of the fingers and the person dropping the ruler. Problems with the ruler drop test include the catcher anticipating the drop from the partner's movements, difficulty reading the scale exactly at the fingers, and results improving with practice.

Reaction times can also be measured with a computer program: the person clicks a mouse or presses a key as soon as the screen changes colour, and the computer records the time. This removes the need to convert a distance to a time and gives a better resolution, and the moment the stimulus appears can be made random. Both tests usually give reaction times of around 0.2 s, which is shorter than a driver's reaction time in an emergency. In a test you are concentrating and expecting the signal, whereas a driver has to notice an unexpected hazard, decide what to do and move their foot to the brake.
keyFacts: Reaction time is the time between seeing a stimulus and responding to it.
Typical reaction times range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Reaction times vary from person to person.
Tiredness, alcohol and drugs increase reaction time.
Distractions, such as using a mobile phone, affect a driver's ability to react.
A longer reaction time gives a longer thinking distance (thinking distance = speed × reaction time).
Reaction time does not affect braking distance.
In the ruler drop test, a greater distance fallen means a longer reaction time.
Repeat measurements and calculate a mean to improve the reliability of reaction time results.

keyTerms.definition: The time between detecting a stimulus and responding to it; typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
The distance a vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time.
A method of measuring reaction time by catching a falling ruler and measuring how far it falls.
A change that a person detects and responds to, such as a ruler being released or a hazard appearing.
The sum of repeat measurements divided by the number of measurements, used to reduce the effect of random errors.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others, often caused by an error; it is left out of the mean.

workedExamples.title: Processing ruler drop results
workedExamples.question: A student's ruler drop results are 16 cm, 18 cm, 31 cm and 17 cm. Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean distance.
steps: 31 cm is much larger than the other three results, so it is anomalous (perhaps the student was not concentrating).

workedExamples.title: Effect of reaction time on thinking distance (with km/h conversion)
workedExamples.question: A tired driver has a reaction time of 0.9 s and is travelling at 54 km/h. Calculate the thinking distance.

workedExamples.title: Comparing alert and distracted reaction times
workedExamples.question: A driver travelling at 30 m/s has a reaction time of 0.5 s when alert and 0.9 s when using a phone. Calculate the extra thinking distance caused by the phone.
workedExamples.answer: 12 m further before braking even starts

workedExamples.title: Converting a ruler drop distance to a time (Higher)
workedExamples.question: A ruler falls 20 cm before it is caught. g = 9.8 m/s². Calculate the reaction time.
steps: The ruler starts at rest (u = 0) and falls s = 0.20 m with a = 9.8 m/s².
a = Δv ÷ t, so t = Δv ÷ a = 1.98 ÷ 9.8.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think alcohol or tiredness increases braking distance.
misconceptions.right: In fact they increase reaction time, so they increase thinking distance. Braking distance depends on speed, the road and the vehicle.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a bigger number on the ruler means faster reactions.
misconceptions.right: In fact a greater distance fallen means the ruler was falling for longer, so the reaction time was longer.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a reaction time measured with a ruler drop is the same as a driver's reaction time.
misconceptions.right: In fact a driver must notice an unexpected hazard, decide and move a foot to the brake, so driving reaction times are usually longer.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think everyone has the same reaction time.
misconceptions.right: In fact reaction times vary between people and for the same person, typically from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

realWorld: Drink-driving and drug-driving laws exist because these substances increase reaction time and thinking distance.
It is illegal to hold a mobile phone while driving in the UK because distraction slows a driver's reactions.
Motorway service stations and road signs encourage tired drivers to take a break every two hours.
Sprinters who react to the starting gun in less than 0.1 s are judged to have false-started, because this is faster than human reaction allows.
higherTier: Converting a ruler drop distance into a reaction time using v² − u² = 2as (with u = 0 and a = 9.8 m/s²) and then t = v ÷ a.
examTips: Learn the typical range: 0.2 s to 0.9 s. Answers such as 2 s or 0.02 s are not sensible.
Link reaction time to thinking distance only, never to braking distance.
When describing the ruler drop test, include: the zero mark level with the fingers, release without warning, read where caught, repeat and take a mean.
When evaluating results, comment on repeatability (spread of results), anomalies and whether the difference between means is bigger than the spread.
Use thinking distance = speed × reaction time, and convert km/h to m/s first.
summary: Reaction time is typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s and varies between people.
Tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions increase reaction time.
Longer reaction time means longer thinking distance and stopping distance.
The ruler drop test measures reaction time from the distance a ruler falls.
Repeat tests, remove anomalies and calculate a mean for reliable results.
Computer tests remove the conversion step and give better resolution.

questions.question: What is the typical range of human reaction times?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.2 s to 0.9 s
questions.explanation: Typical reaction times are 0.2 s to 0.9 s. A few thousandths of a second is far too quick for a person, and 2 s or more would be extremely slow.

questions.question: Which of these would NOT increase a driver's reaction time?
markScheme: 1 mark: Being well rested and concentrating
questions.explanation: Tiredness, alcohol and distractions such as a phone all increase reaction time. A rested, focused driver reacts fastest.

questions.question: A driver's reaction time increases. Which distance increases as a direct result?
options: Neither the thinking distance nor the braking distance
markScheme: 1 mark: The thinking distance
questions.explanation: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so a longer reaction time gives a longer thinking distance. Braking distance does not depend on reaction time.

questions.question:
Two students, X and Y, did a ruler drop test.
Table 1 shows the distance the ruler fell before each student caught it.
What can you conclude?
options: Student Y has the shorter reaction time.
Student X has the shorter reaction time.
Both students have the same reaction time.
markScheme: 1 mark: Student X has the shorter reaction time.
questions.explanation: The ruler falls further the longer it takes to catch it, so the smaller distance (12 cm) means the shorter reaction time. Both rulers fall with the same acceleration.

questions.question: Why should a student repeat the ruler drop test several times and calculate a mean?
options: To make the ruler fall faster
To remove the need to convert distance to time
To reduce the effect of random errors and identify anomalies
To make sure the reaction time is exactly 0.2 s
markScheme: 1 mark: To reduce the effect of random errors and identify anomalies
questions.explanation: Individual reaction times vary. Repeating lets you spot anomalous results and the mean is a better estimate of the true value.

questions.question:
Two students compare their reaction times using a ruler drop test.
Which is the most important control variable?
options: The starting position of the catcher's fingers (level with zero)
markScheme: 1 mark: The starting position of the catcher's fingers (level with zero)
questions.explanation: If the fingers start at different positions, the distance read from the scale would not be the distance fallen. The mass and colour of the ruler do not affect how fast it falls or the measurement.

questions.question:
A computer test measures reaction time. The user clicks the mouse when the screen changes colour.
What is an advantage of using the computer test rather than a ruler drop test?
options: It records the time directly with a better resolution, and the stimulus can appear at random times.
It always gives a reaction time of 0.9 s.
It does not need repeat measurements.
It measures the braking distance of a car.
markScheme: 1 mark: It records the time directly with a better resolution, and the stimulus can appear at random times.
questions.explanation: The computer measures time to the nearest millisecond and cannot give clues about when the stimulus appears. Repeats are still needed because reaction times vary.

questions.question:
The speed of a car doubles. The reaction time of the driver also doubles because the driver is tired.
By what factor does the thinking distance change?
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases four times.
questions.explanation: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Doubling both gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the thinking distance.

questions.question: Which value is the most sensible estimate of a typical driver's reaction time in an emergency?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.7 s
questions.explanation: 0.7 s is within the typical range of 0.2 s to 0.9 s. The Highway Code thinking distances assume a reaction time of about 0.7 s.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of a student's ruler drop test.
What is the best value to use for the mean distance?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12.3 cm
questions.explanation: 25 cm is anomalous, so it is left out. Mean = (12 + 13 + 12) ÷ 3 = 12.3 cm. 15.5 cm includes the anomaly; 12 cm is the mode, not the mean.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of a student's ruler drop test.
Calculate the mean distance the ruler fell.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 cm
questions.explanation: Mean = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 cm.

questions.question:
A driver is travelling at 13 m/s. The reaction time of the driver is 0.5 s.
Calculate the thinking distance.
markScheme: 1 mark: 6.5 m
questions.explanation: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 13 × 0.5 = 6.5 m.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of three computer reaction tests.
Calculate the mean reaction time.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.27 s

questions.question:
A driver travels at 30 m/s.
Table 1 shows the reaction time of the driver when she is alert and when she is using a phone.
Calculate how much further the car travels before the brakes are applied when she is using the phone.
markScheme: 1 mark: alert thinking distance = 30 × 0.5 = 15 m
1 mark: distracted thinking distance = 30 × 0.9 = 27 m
1 mark: difference = 12 m
questions.explanation: 27 − 15 = 12 m, or 30 × (0.9 − 0.5) = 12 m. That is about three car lengths further before braking even starts.

questions.question:
A ruler is released from rest. The ruler falls 20 cm before it is caught.
The acceleration of the ruler is 9.8 m/s².
Calculate the reaction time of the person catching the ruler.
Use the equation:
(final velocity)² − (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance
markScheme: 1 mark: v = 1.98 m/s
1 mark: t = 0.20 s
questions.explanation: Use v² − u² = 2as with u = 0 to find the final speed, then a = Δv ÷ t to find the time. Remember to convert 20 cm to 0.20 m.

questions.question:
A metre rule is released from rest. The rule falls 45 cm before it is caught.
The acceleration of the rule is 9.8 m/s².
Calculate the reaction time of the person catching the rule.
Use the equation:
(final velocity)² − (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance
markScheme: 1 mark: v = 2.97 m/s
1 mark: t = 0.30 s
questions.explanation: v = √8.82 = 2.97 m/s; t = 2.97 ÷ 9.8 = 0.30 s. This is longer than the 20 cm result, as expected for a greater distance fallen.

questions.question:
A driver is travelling at 54 km/h. The reaction time of the driver is 0.9 s.
Calculate the thinking distance.
markScheme: 1 mark: 13.5 m
questions.explanation: Convert first: 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Thinking distance = 15 × 0.9 = 13.5 m.

questions.question:
A car travels at 27 m/s.
Table 1 shows the reaction time of the driver when alert and when tired.
Calculate the extra thinking distance when the driver is tired.
markScheme: 1 mark: alert: 27 × 0.4 = 10.8 m
1 mark: tired: 27 × 0.8 = 21.6 m
1 mark: extra = 10.8 m
questions.explanation: Doubling the reaction time doubles the thinking distance, from 10.8 m to 21.6 m, an extra 10.8 m.

questions.question: State the typical range of human reaction times.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.2 s to 0.9 s
questions.explanation: This range is given in the AQA specification and should be learned.

questions.question: Give two factors that can increase a driver's reaction time.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: tiredness; alcohol; drugs (including some medicines); distractions (such as using a phone)
questions.explanation: These factors slow the brain's processing or reduce attention, so the driver responds later.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a ruler drop test.
Describe how the ruler drop test can be used to measure a person's reaction time.
markScheme: 1 mark: partner holds ruler vertically with the zero mark level with the catcher's open thumb and finger
1 mark: partner releases the ruler without warning and the catcher catches it; read the distance fallen at the fingers
1 mark: repeat several times, calculate a mean and convert distance to time using a table or graph
questions.explanation: A longer distance fallen means a longer reaction time. Repeating improves the reliability of the result.

questions.question: Explain why using a mobile phone while driving increases the stopping distance of a car.
markScheme: 1 mark: the driver is distracted, so reaction time increases
1 mark: so the thinking distance increases (stopping distance = thinking + braking distance)
questions.explanation: The car travels further at full speed before the brakes are applied. The braking distance is unchanged.

questions.question: Suggest why reaction times measured with a ruler drop test are usually shorter than a driver's reaction time in an emergency.
markScheme: 1 mark: in the test the person is concentrating and expecting the stimulus
1 mark: a driver must notice an unexpected hazard, decide what to do and move a foot to the brake pedal
questions.explanation: The ruler test measures a simple, expected response using the fingers. Driving involves more steps.

questions.question:
A student says: "Drinking alcohol increases a car's braking distance."
Evaluate this statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: alcohol increases reaction time, so it increases thinking distance
1 mark: braking distance depends on speed, road and vehicle conditions, so it is not affected; the statement is incorrect (although stopping distance does increase)
questions.explanation: Alcohol does make stopping distance longer, but through thinking distance, not braking distance.

questions.question:
Evaluate the ruler drop test as a method of measuring reaction time.
Give one strength, one weakness and one improvement.
markScheme: 1 mark: strength: simple, quick and cheap, using everyday equipment
1 mark: weakness: catcher may anticipate the release from the partner's movement; or hard to read the scale exactly at the fingers; or results improve with practice
1 mark: improvement: repeat and take a mean; same person drops each time with random delays; or use a computer-based test
questions.explanation: A good evaluation links each weakness to how it affects the result and suggests a specific improvement.

questions.question:
A student did ten ruler drop tests.
Table 1 shows the results.
Suggest a reason for the pattern in the results.
Suggest how the method could be improved.
markScheme: 1 mark: she is learning or getting used to the test (practice effect), or learning to anticipate the release
1 mark: allow some practice attempts before recording, or vary the delay before release randomly
questions.explanation: A trend in repeat results suggests a systematic change, not just random variation, so the method should be adjusted.

questions.question:
Plan an investigation to find out whether listening to loud music affects a person's reaction time.
Use a ruler drop test.
Include the variables and how you would make sure the results are valid.
markScheme: Indicative content: independent variable is music on or off (or volume); dependent variable is reaction time (distance fallen converted to time); control variables: same person catching, same hand, same ruler, same person dropping, fingers start level with zero, same gap between thumb and finger, same seating position; method: partner holds ruler with zero at catcher's fingers, releases without warning, record distance where caught, repeat at least 5 times without music and 5 times with music; remove anomalies, calculate means, convert to time using a conversion table; allow practice attempts first; compare means and spread; a longer mean time with music shows that distraction increases reaction time.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed method that would produce valid results, with correct independent, dependent and several control variables and repeats with a mean.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with some detail and some correct variables; repeats may be missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about catching a ruler with and without music.
questions.explanation: Include clear variables, a fair test (only the music changes), repeats and a way of processing the data.

questions.question: Explain how tiredness, alcohol and distractions can affect the stopping distance of a car.
markScheme: Indicative content: each factor increases the driver's reaction time (tiredness slows responses; alcohol and drugs slow the brain's processing; distractions mean the hazard is noticed later); thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so thinking distance increases; braking distance is not affected by these factors; stopping distance = thinking + braking distance, so stopping distance increases; the effect is greater at higher speeds.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links the factors to increased reaction time and thinking distance, and so increased stopping distance, noting that braking distance is unchanged.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the factors make it take longer to stop, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: The chain is: factor → longer reaction time → longer thinking distance → longer stopping distance.

questions.question:
Two students, A and B, each did three computer reaction tests.
Table 1 shows the results.
Student A says:
"I have a faster reaction time than Student B."
Evaluate this conclusion.
Use data from Table 1 in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: mean for A = 0.22 s; mean for B including all results = 0.23 s, which would support the claim; but B's results have a large spread and 0.31 s looks anomalous; mean for B without the anomaly = 0.19 s, which is faster than A; A's results are more repeatable; the difference between the means is small compared with the spread, so the conclusion is not secure; more repeats are needed for both students.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): calculates means, identifies the anomaly and its effect, and gives a justified judgement about the conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): compares some values or calculates one mean, with a simple judgement.
questions.explanation: Whether a conclusion is valid depends on the spread of the data and on how anomalies are treated, not just on comparing two means.
